title: Vocabulary & Grammar
description: Growing a rich word bank and understanding how words work together. Early stages build oral vocabulary through categories, opposites and describing words; later stages develop grammar (word classes, sentence structure, tense) and word knowledge (roots, connotation, register).

stages.overview: Naming the world: word categories, describing words and opposites through talk and play.
goals: Use describing words for size, colour and feeling

units.title: Words That Belong Together
units.summary: Grouping words helps us remember and understand them.
objectives: Sort familiar words into categories
Explain why one word does not belong in a group
masteryCriteria: Sorts objects into at least four categories
Identifies and explains the odd one out
Names several members of common categories

revision.notes: Revisit through play: replay one activity, retell the story, and do one hands-on task. Keep revision under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: Odd One Out
objectives: Sort familiar words into categories
Explain why one word does not belong in a group
explanation: Words can live together in groups called categories. Dog, cat and cow are all animals. Banana, rice and roti are all food.
When one word does not fit a group, it is the odd one out. In "apple, mango, car", car is the odd one out because it is not a fruit.
Knowing categories helps your brain store new words. When you learn the word "parrot", you can put it in the bird group.

vocabulary.meaning: a group of things that are alike
the one that does not belong

examples: Shirt, socks, cap — all clothes.
Bus, train, boat — all vehicles.

story.title: Tara Sorts the Shelf
story.text: Tara the tortoise was tidying the shop shelves. She put the mangoes with the bananas, the shoes with the socks. Then she found a little toy car among the fruits. "You don't belong here!" Tara laughed, and carried it carefully to the toy shelf.

activities.prompt: Which is the odd one out? 🐶 🐱 🚗
Match the word to its group
Train and boat are both vehicles.

thinking: Can a word belong to two groups? (Is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable?)
Why might it help to know which group a word belongs to?
speaking: Name five animals, five foods and five things to wear, and tell a grown-up which was hardest.

project.title: Category Sorting Mats
steps: Label three mats: animals, food, clothes (with pictures)
Gather 12 objects or toy figures
Sort each one onto the right mat
Add one odd one out and ask a grown-up to find it

assessment.prompt: A sock is a kind of food.

mastery: Sorts objects into at least four categories
Identifies and explains the odd one out
Names several members of common categories

units.title: Describing Words and Opposites
units.summary: Words that tell us more, and words that mean the opposite.
objectives: Use describing words for size, temperature, speed and feeling
Name the opposite of common describing words
masteryCriteria: Uses a range of describing words in talk
Gives opposites for at least 10 common words
Uses comparisons like big/small accurately

revision.notes: Revisit through play: replay one activity, retell the story, and do one hands-on task. Keep revision under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: Big and Small, Hot and Cold
objectives: Use describing words for size, temperature, speed and feeling
Name the opposite of common describing words
explanation: Describing words tell us more about something. Not just "a dog" but "a big, fluffy dog". Describing words make our talking and writing more exciting.
Many describing words have an opposite — a word that means the very different thing. Hot and cold. Fast and slow. Up and down. Full and empty.
We can use opposites to compare: the elephant is big, but the mouse is small.

vocabulary.meaning: a word with the very different meaning
look at how things are alike or different

examples: Ice is cold; tea is hot.
A cheetah is fast; a snail is slow.

story.title: Fast Kiko, Slow Tara
story.text: Kiko the goat raced up the hill — fast, fast, fast! Tara the tortoise walked — slow, slow, slow. At the top, Kiko was tired and hot. Tara arrived cool and calm. "Fast and slow are opposites," said Tara, "but we both got to the top!"

thinking: Is a cat big or small? (It depends! Compared to what?)
Does every word have an opposite? What is the opposite of "banana"?
speaking: Describe your favourite toy using three describing words.

project.title: Opposites Hunt Photo Book
steps: Find pairs of opposites at home: full and empty cup, open and closed door
Draw or photograph each pair
Make a little book with one pair per page
Read it to someone, saying both words

mastery: Uses a range of describing words in talk
Gives opposites for at least 10 common words
Uses comparisons like big/small accurately

stages.overview: Nouns, verbs and adjectives; plurals; and growing vocabulary from stories.
goals: Identify nouns (naming words) and verbs (doing words)
Learn and use new words from stories

units.title: Naming Words and Doing Words
units.summary: Nouns name things; verbs tell what happens.
objectives: Identify nouns and verbs in simple sentences
Build a sentence with a noun and a verb
masteryCriteria: Identifies nouns and verbs in simple sentences
Generates examples of each
Explains the difference between naming and doing words

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: Nouns and Verbs
objectives: Identify nouns and verbs in simple sentences
Build a sentence with a noun and a verb
explanation: Nouns are naming words. They name people (teacher), places (school), animals (tiger) and things (pencil). If you can put "a" or "the" in front of it, it is often a noun.
Verbs are doing words. They tell us the action: run, jump, eat, sing, sleep. If you can do it, it's probably a verb.
Most sentences need both: "The dog barks." Dog is the noun — who; barks is the verb — what it does.

vocabulary.meaning: a naming word for a person, place, animal or thing
words that make a complete idea

examples: "Birds fly." — birds (noun), fly (verb).
"Ivaan kicks the ball." — Ivaan, ball (nouns); kicks (verb).

story.title: The Word Party
story.text: At the word party, the nouns arrived: tiger, cake, Momo, garden. They stood still. Then the verbs arrived: dance, jump, eat! Suddenly everything happened. "The tiger dances! Momo eats cake!" The nouns needed the verbs to have any fun.

activities.prompt: Match each word to what kind of word it is
pairs: a naming word for an animal
a naming word for a place

thinking: Can one word be both a noun and a verb? (Think about "a fish" and "to fish".)
Why do sentences need verbs?
speaking: Act out five verbs and ask someone to guess them, then name the noun doing each action.

project.title: Noun–Verb Silly Sentences
steps: Write 6 nouns on slips in one cup and 6 verbs in another
Pull one from each cup
Say the sentence: "The elephant sings!"
Draw your silliest sentence

assessment.prompt: In "The cat sleeps", the verb is…

mastery: Identifies nouns and verbs in simple sentences
Generates examples of each
Explains the difference between naming and doing words

units.title: One and Many
units.summary: Plurals: how words change when there is more than one.
objectives: Form plurals by adding -s or -es
Recognise some irregular plurals
masteryCriteria: Forms regular -s/-es plurals correctly
Knows common irregular plurals
Uses plurals accurately in speech and writing

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: One Cat, Two Cats
objectives: Form plurals by adding -s or -es
Recognise some irregular plurals
explanation: A plural means more than one. Usually we just add -s: one cat, two cats; one book, three books.
If a word ends in s, x, sh or ch, we add -es so we can say it easily: bus → buses, box → boxes, dish → dishes, lunch → lunches.
A few words are rule-breakers: one child, two children; one mouse, two mice; one foot, two feet. We just have to learn these.
examples: One fox, two foxes.
One tooth, many teeth.

story.title: The Mice and the Mouses
story.text: Kiko counted the visitors: "One mouse, two mouses!" The mice giggled. "We are mice, not mouses!" they squeaked. "Some words have their own special plural." Kiko blushed and counted again: "One mouse, two mice, three mice!"

thinking: Why do you think we add -es to "bus" instead of just -s?
Can you find a word that stays the same in the plural? (Think: sheep.)
speaking: Count things around you and say each plural aloud, like "three spoons, two dishes".

project.title: Plural Shop
steps: Set up a pretend shop with groups of objects
Make labels: "1 box", "3 boxes"
Take turns buying, saying the singular or plural correctly
Find one rule-breaker word to sell

mastery: Forms regular -s/-es plurals correctly
Knows common irregular plurals
Uses plurals accurately in speech and writing

stages.overview: Adjectives and adverbs, synonyms, and the past and present tense.
goals: Use adjectives and adverbs to add detail
Use past and present tense consistently

units.title: Wow Words and Synonyms
objectives: Find synonyms for common words
Order synonyms by strength (shades of meaning)
masteryCriteria: Generates synonyms for common words
Orders words by intensity
Selects precise words in writing

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Shades of Meaning
objectives: Find synonyms for common words
Order synonyms by strength (shades of meaning)
prerequisites: Knows nouns, verbs and describing words
explanation: Synonyms are words with similar meanings: big, large, huge, enormous. But they are not exactly the same — some are stronger than others.
We can line synonyms up from weakest to strongest: warm → hot → boiling. Choosing the right "shade" makes your meaning precise.
Writers swap tired words like "nice" or "said" for more exact ones: "The soup was delicious." "She whispered."

vocabulary.meaning: a word with a similar meaning
how strong or gentle a word is compared with similar words

examples: Said: whispered, shouted, asked, giggled.
Small: little, tiny, minuscule.

story.title: Nice, Nice, Nice
story.text: Momo wrote: "We had a nice day. The weather was nice. The food was nice." Rangi said, "Nice is tired! Let's wake it up." Together they wrote: "We had a wonderful day. The weather was sunny and warm. The food was delicious." Momo grinned — it sounded like a real adventure now.

thinking: Are "slim" and "skinny" exactly the same? How might someone feel hearing each?
Why might a writer choose a simple word on purpose?
speaking: Tell someone about your lunch using three exact describing words instead of "nice" or "good".

project.title: Word Thermometer
steps: Draw a thermometer on a strip
Pick a word family (cold → freezing)
Write words from gentle at the bottom to strong at the top
Make two more thermometers for "happy" and "big"

assessment.prompt: Synonyms always mean exactly the same thing.

mastery: Generates synonyms for common words
Orders words by intensity
Selects precise words in writing

units.title: Past, Present and Future
units.summary: Verbs change to show when things happen.
objectives: Use present and past tense verbs correctly
Keep the same tense throughout a short piece
masteryCriteria: Uses regular and common irregular past forms
Maintains consistent tense in writing
Identifies past, present and future sentences

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: When Did It Happen?
objectives: Use present and past tense verbs correctly
Keep the same tense throughout a short piece
explanation: Verbs tell us WHEN something happens. Present tense: it is happening now — "I play." Past tense: it already happened — "I played." Future: it will happen — "I will play."
Many past tense verbs add -ed: jump → jumped, walk → walked. Some are irregular: go → went, see → saw, eat → ate, run → ran.
When we write a story or recount, we usually stay in one tense. Switching tense by accident confuses readers.

vocabulary.meaning: the form of a verb that shows time

examples: Today I walk to school. Yesterday I walked to school. Tomorrow I will walk to school.
go → went; swim → swam; catch → caught.

story.title: The Time-Travelling Verb
story.text: Bolt built a time machine for verbs. "Play" stepped inside. Whoosh — it zoomed to yesterday and came out as "played"! Whoosh — to tomorrow: "will play"! Then "go" went in and came out as "went". "Some verbs change their whole costume," Bolt beeped.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is in the future?

thinking: Why do you think some verbs are irregular?
When might a writer switch tense on purpose?
speaking: Tell someone what you did yesterday, what you are doing now, and what you will do tomorrow.

project.title: Timeline of My Day
steps: Draw a line with "yesterday", "today" and "tomorrow"
Write one sentence for each in the correct tense
Underline the verbs
Read it aloud and check the tenses

assessment.prompt: "I will eat" is in the past tense.

mastery: Uses regular and common irregular past forms
Maintains consistent tense in writing
Identifies past, present and future sentences

stages.overview: Grammar for meaning: sentence types, clauses, pronouns and punctuation.
goals: Write statements, questions, commands and exclamations
Use pronouns to avoid repetition clearly
Use commas, apostrophes and speech marks

units.title: Four Kinds of Sentences
objectives: Identify and write statements, questions, commands and exclamations
Punctuate each sentence type correctly
masteryCriteria: Writes and punctuates all four sentence types
Explains the purpose of each type
Uses sentence types purposefully in writing

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Sentence Jobs
objectives: Identify and write statements, questions, commands and exclamations
Punctuate each sentence type correctly
prerequisites: Writes sentences with capitals and full stops
explanation: A statement tells you something: "Elephants are the largest land animals." It ends with a full stop.
A question asks something and ends with a question mark: "Where do penguins live?" A command tells someone to do something, often starting with a bossy verb: "Close the door."
An exclamation shows strong feeling or surprise and ends with an exclamation mark. In grammar, a "true" exclamation often starts with What or How: "What a huge wave that was!"

vocabulary.meaning: a sentence that shows strong feeling

examples: Command: "Mix the flour and water."
Exclamation: "How brave you were!"

story.title: The Four Friends
story.text: Four sentence friends lived in a book. Statement said calm facts. Question kept wondering, "Why? How?" Command bossed everyone: "Line up!" And Exclamation shouted, "Wow, what a day!" Together, they made the book come alive.

activities.prompt: Match the sentence to its type
Which ends with a question mark?
Commands often start with a verb.

thinking: Can a question be rude or polite depending on how it is asked?
Why do recipes use so many commands?
speaking: Give a friend directions to an object in your house using only commands.

project.title: Sentence-Type Recipe Card
steps: Choose a simple snack to make
Write the instructions as commands
Add a question at the top ("Are you hungry?")
Add a statement fact and an exclamation
Label each sentence type

assessment.prompt: "How tall that tree is!" is a…
"Please pass the salt." is a command.

mastery: Writes and punctuates all four sentence types
Explains the purpose of each type
Uses sentence types purposefully in writing

units.title: Commas, Apostrophes and Speech
objectives: Use apostrophes for contractions
Use apostrophes to show possession
masteryCriteria: Uses contractions correctly
Places possessive apostrophes correctly for singular and plural nouns
Distinguishes its and it's

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: The Apostrophe's Two Jobs
objectives: Use apostrophes for contractions
Use apostrophes to show possession
explanation: An apostrophe has two jobs. Job one: contraction — showing where letters are missing when two words squash together. do not → don't; it is → it's; I am → I'm.
Job two: possession — showing something belongs to someone. The dog's bone (one dog). With plural nouns ending in s, the apostrophe goes after the s: the dogs' bones (many dogs).
Watch out: "its" (belonging to it) has NO apostrophe: "The cat licked its paw." "It's" always means "it is" or "it has".

vocabulary.meaning: the mark ' used for contractions and possession

examples: can not → can't; we will → we'll.
Riya's book (belongs to Riya); the girls' team (belongs to the girls).

story.title: The Apostrophe Who Did Two Jobs
story.text: Little Apostrophe worked in two places. In the morning it stood where letters had left: "I'm late!" In the afternoon it guarded belongings: "That's Kiko's hat!" "I'm small," it said, "but without me, nobody knows who owns what!"

activities.prompt: Match the words to the contraction
The bone belongs to one dog:
"The boys' bikes" means bikes belonging to more than one boy.

thinking: Why might people often confuse "its" and "it's"?
How does the apostrophe change the meaning in "my sister's friends" and "my sisters' friends"?
speaking: Explain the two jobs of an apostrophe to someone using examples from your home.

project.title: Apostrophe Hunt
steps: Find 10 apostrophes in real texts
Highlight contractions in one colour and possession in another
Write the full form of each contraction
Look for any mistakes on signs or menus in your area

mastery: Uses contractions correctly
Places possessive apostrophes correctly for singular and plural nouns
Distinguishes its and it's

stages.overview: Word origins, figurative language, and complex sentences with clauses.
goals: Use Latin and Greek roots to understand words
Construct complex sentences with subordinate and relative clauses

units.title: Word Roots and Origins
units.summary: English borrows from many languages, including Sanskrit.
objectives: Use common Greek and Latin roots to infer meanings
Recognise English words borrowed from Indian languages
masteryCriteria: Uses roots to infer meanings of unfamiliar words
Identifies loanwords and their source languages
Uses a dictionary to trace etymology

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Roots and Borrowed Words
objectives: Use common Greek and Latin roots to infer meanings
Recognise English words borrowed from Indian languages
explanation: Many English words are built from ancient Greek and Latin roots. "Tele" (far) + "phone" (sound) = telephone. "Bio" (life) + "logy" (study) = biology. "Port" (carry) appears in transport, export, portable.

English has borrowed thousands of words from other languages. From Hindi and other Indian languages: shampoo, bungalow, jungle, pyjamas, verandah (also via Portuguese), thug. From Sanskrit, often through Hindi: avatar, karma, guru, mantra, yoga.
Etymology is the study of where words come from. Dictionaries often list a word's origin, which can help you remember its meaning.

context.text: Words like "shampoo" (from Hindi chāmpo, "press/massage") and "bungalow" (from bangla, "of Bengal") entered English during the colonial period; their histories are recorded in historical dictionaries such as the Oxford English Dictionary.

vocabulary.meaning: the core part of a word carrying meaning
a word borrowed from another language

examples: "Aqua" (water): aquarium, aquatic.
"Graph" (write): autograph, paragraph, photograph.

story.title: The Word Passport
story.text: Nova gave each word a passport. "Jungle" showed stamps from Sanskrit (jaṅgala, meaning dry, uncultivated land) to Hindi to English. "Telescope" had Greek stamps: tele (far) and skopein (to look). "Every word," said Nova, "has travelled to reach us."

activities.prompt: Match the root to its meaning
Which English word comes from Hindi?
English has borrowed words from many languages.

thinking: Why do languages borrow words from each other?
What does it tell us about history when one language borrows many words from another?
speaking: Teach someone three roots and five words built from them.

project.title: Etymology Detective Journal
materials: a dictionary with etymologies (print or offline app)
steps: Choose 10 interesting words
Look up each word's origin
Draw a "word journey" map for three of them
Find two English words that came from an Indian language

mastery: Uses roots to infer meanings of unfamiliar words
Identifies loanwords and their source languages
Uses a dictionary to trace etymology

units.title: Figurative Language and Idioms
units.summary: Language that means more than the literal words.
objectives: Distinguish literal from figurative meaning
Interpret and use similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole and idioms
masteryCriteria: Identifies figurative devices accurately
Explains the intended meaning and effect
Uses figurative language purposefully in writing

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Not Literally!
objectives: Distinguish literal from figurative meaning
Interpret and use similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole and idioms
explanation: Literal language means exactly what the words say. Figurative language uses words in imaginative ways to create a picture or feeling.

A simile compares using "like" or "as" (as brave as a lion). A metaphor says something IS something else (the classroom was a zoo). Personification gives human qualities to non-human things (the wind howled). Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration (I've told you a million times).
Idioms are phrases whose meaning cannot be worked out from the words: "it's raining cats and dogs", "a piece of cake". Every language has its own idioms.

vocabulary.meaning: meaning exactly what the words say
a phrase whose meaning differs from its words

examples: "Her smile was sunshine" — metaphor.
"Break a leg!" — idiom meaning good luck.

story.title: Bolt Takes Everything Literally
story.text: Rangi said, "It's raining cats and dogs!" Bolt rushed outside with a basket to catch them. Then Kiko said, "This homework is a piece of cake." Bolt looked for a fork. Nova laughed: "They're idioms, Bolt. They mean heavy rain and very easy!"

activities.prompt: Match the example to the device
pairs: I'm so hungry I could eat a horse

activities.prompt: "The sun smiled down on us" is personification.

thinking: Why don't idioms translate well between languages? Can you think of an idiom in Marathi or Hindi?
Is figurative language ever confusing for readers? How should writers handle that?
speaking: Describe a storm using one simile, one metaphor and one example of personification.

project.title: Idiom Picture Book
steps: Choose 6 idioms
Draw the silly literal meaning on one side
Write the real meaning on the other
Add one idiom from another language you know, with its translation

assessment.prompt: "Her voice was music to my ears" is a…
"I've walked a thousand miles today!" is…

mastery: Identifies figurative devices accurately
Explains the intended meaning and effect
Uses figurative language purposefully in writing

stages.overview: Language in context: register, connotation, grammar for style, and how language changes.
goals: Adapt register for audience and purpose
Understand how languages change over time

units.title: Register and Style
units.summary: Choosing language to fit audience, purpose and context.
objectives: Shift between formal and informal registers
Use active and passive voice deliberately
masteryCriteria: Adapts register appropriately across contexts
Uses active and passive voice for effect
Analyses how grammar choices position readers

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Register, Active and Passive Voice
objectives: Shift between formal and informal registers
Use active and passive voice deliberately
explanation: Register is the level of formality of language. Texting a friend ("gonna be late lol") uses informal register; an email to a principal ("I will be arriving late") uses formal register. Skilled writers move between registers deliberately.
In active voice, the subject does the action: "The committee rejected the plan." In passive voice, the subject receives the action: "The plan was rejected (by the committee)."

Passive voice is useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant, common in scientific writing ("The solution was heated"). It can also hide responsibility ("Mistakes were made") — a reason readers should notice it.
examples: Informal: "Loads of people turned up." Formal: "Attendance was high."
Active: "Scientists discovered the virus." Passive: "The virus was discovered."

story.title: Mistakes Were Made
story.text: After the school fair lost money, two reports were written. One said: "The treasurer forgot to collect entry fees." The other said: "Entry fees were not collected." The students debated: both were true, but one named who was responsible and one did not. Grammar, they realised, can shape blame.

options: The ball was chased by the dog.

activities.prompt: Passive voice can hide who is responsible.

thinking: Is formal language always better? When might informal be more effective?
Why do scientific reports often use the passive voice?
speaking: Explain the same event (e.g. a broken window) to a friend, a teacher and a newspaper, changing your register each time.

project.title: Register Remix
materials: a short informal text (message or diary entry)
steps: Choose an informal text
Rewrite it as a formal report
Rewrite it as a children's story
Annotate the changes in vocabulary, sentence structure and voice
Reflect on what each version gains and loses

assessment.prompt: "The window was broken." The doer is…
Active voice usually makes it clear who did the action.

mastery: Adapts register appropriately across contexts
Uses active and passive voice for effect
Analyses how grammar choices position readers

units.title: Connotation and Language Change
units.summary: Words carry associations, and languages keep evolving.
objectives: Distinguish denotation from connotation
Explain how and why word meanings change over time
masteryCriteria: Analyses connotation and loaded language in real texts
Explains processes of language change with examples
Chooses words deliberately for connotation

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Denotation, Connotation and Change
objectives: Distinguish denotation from connotation
Explain how and why word meanings change over time
explanation: Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feelings and associations it carries. "Thrifty" and "stingy" both denote careful spending, but thrifty sounds positive and stingy sounds negative.

Loaded language uses strong connotations to influence opinion; euphemisms soften harsh realities ("passed away" for "died"). Recognising these helps readers think critically about news and advertising.
Languages change constantly. New words appear (selfie, podcast), meanings shift (in older English "nice" once meant "foolish"), and words are borrowed. Change is normal, not decay.

context.text: Historical dictionaries record that "nice" came from Latin nescius ("ignorant") and meant "foolish" in Middle English before gradually shifting to its modern positive meaning.

vocabulary.meaning: a mild word used instead of a harsh one
a shift in a word's meaning over time

examples: "Home" vs "house": same denotation, warmer connotation for home.
"Freedom fighter" vs "rebel" — loaded language shaping how a group is seen.

story.title: The Word That Changed Its Mind
story.text: Professor Hoot read an old book aloud: "He was a nice fellow" — meaning foolish! The class gasped. "Words drift," said Hoot. "In a few hundred years, people may laugh at how we use words today."

activities.prompt: Which has the most positive connotation?
Word meanings can change over time.

thinking: Is it a problem that words change meaning? Who decides what a word means?
How might two newspapers describe the same protest with different connotations?
speaking: Describe a classmate's confidence positively and negatively using only connotation changes, then discuss the effect.

project.title: News Language Analysis
materials: two news articles on the same event from different sources
steps: Highlight emotionally loaded words in each
List the connotations of each word
Identify any euphemisms
Write a 400-word comparison of how language shapes the reader's view

assessment.prompt: The dictionary meaning of a word is its…
Euphemisms make harsh things sound gentler.

mastery: Analyses connotation and loaded language in real texts
Explains processes of language change with examples
Chooses words deliberately for connotation
